subject: Careers
title: Attendance, punctuality and reliability
objective_verbatim: I can explain why being on time matters and choose an appropriate action if I am delayed or absent.
outcomes_verbatim: I can explain why being on time matters and choose an appropriate action if I am delayed or absent.
calendar_note: Year A. Spring 2 Week 2, 2027-03-01 to 2027-03-05. Tuesday 2 March 2027, Tuesday P3. One 40-minute lesson. Spring 2 runs 22 February to Thursday 25 March 2027. Week 5 is four days with no Friday; the Tuesday lesson is unaffected.

outcomes_verbatim: I can explain why being on time matters and choose an appropriate action if I am delayed or absent.
sources.note: The current brief supplies the exact focuses, outcomes and row mapping. Other scheme columns are not asserted verbatim. Activities and 40-minute sequencing are newly authored in the accepted Spring 1 format.
Read for file shape, timing, tiers, feedback, private response and typed/scribed access conventions.
Read for the six-outcome closing Evidence Sheet grid pattern. Current six outcomes are rows 22–27 and current Week 5 combines rows 26–27.

source_adaptation: Exact owner-supplied focus and outcomes retained. Rows 26 and 27 share the closing Week 5 lesson. Newly authored invented workplace practice, not a quotation of absent sequence/evidence columns.
timing: Use a calm check-in. Read the goal aloud. Explain that these are made-up work tasks, not pupils’ attendance records. Recall one work skill. Read aloud a 9:00 team start and arrivals of 8:55 and 9:10. Ask which gives time to get ready.

Model the delayed-worker example. Explain two effects of time: the team can plan and a task can start safely. Model telling the agreed contact as soon as safe, using the agreed way, and following the next instruction. Check: 'Must I rush or take a risk if I am late?'

Use the four scenario cards. For each, ask what the worker should do and why. Distinguish delay from absence. Rehearse a short factual message without personal or medical details. Ask the hinge question with simultaneous pointing or choice cards. If any pupil waits silently or chooses rushing, model a safe contact message and use the parallel hinge. If secure, remove the message stem for a new delay.
Offer the three routes. Require one reason why time matters, one delay action and one absence action. Let pupils dictate, draw or write in books. Record the support actually used.

Compare a silent delay with an early message. Ask which lets the team plan and why. Revisit the success criteria. Give each pupil one attainable next step. Ask the exit prompt. Record a short evidence note. Reinforce that illness and travel problems may happen; the taught skill is using safe, agreed communication, not blame.
timing_basis: Accepted Spring 1 Careers format: 5 + 8 + 10 + 12 + 5 = 40. Processing time and short pauses sit inside the total. Slides marked same task time share the 12-minute independent block.

routes.Supported: In your book: choose a reason why time helps. Match a late card and an away card to the right action. Point, draw or tell an adult your answers.
routes.Independent: In your book: give one reason to be ready on time. Write or say a short delay message. Choose what to do if absent. Use the agreed contact and steps.
routes.Aspire: In your book: give two reasons time matters. Plan a delay message and an absence message. Add what to do if the first message gets no reply and there is an agreed next step.

cases.title: Ready to start
cases.situation: A team in a made-up packing room starts at 9:00. A worker is there at 8:55 and follows the agreed steps to get ready.
cases.question: Why does being ready on time help? Choose a reason: The team can plan. / No one needs to plan.
cases.answer: The team can plan and start the task together.
cases.reason: Other workers know who is there and can share the tasks safely.

cases.title: The late bus
cases.situation: A worker's bus is held up. The worker may miss the start time.
cases.question: What should the worker do? Choose: Stay safe and tell the agreed contact now. / Rush and say nothing.
cases.answer: When safe, tell the agreed contact as soon as possible, using the agreed way. Say they are delayed, give an arrival estimate only if known, and follow the reply.
cases.reason: A clear early message helps the team change its plan. The worker must not rush or guess a time.

cases.title: Away today
cases.situation: A worker cannot come in today. The workplace has agreed absence steps.
cases.question: What should the worker do? Choose: Use the absence steps and tell the contact. / Wait until tomorrow.
cases.answer: Use the agreed absence steps and tell the agreed contact as soon as possible. Ask a trusted adult for support if needed.
cases.reason: The team needs to know the worker is absent. A pupil does not need to share private health details in this role play.

cases.title: No reply yet
cases.situation: A worker has sent a delay message in the agreed way. There is no reply. The workplace has a next contact step.
cases.question: What should the worker do?
cases.answer: Follow the agreed next contact step when safe, or ask a trusted adult for help. Do not assume the message has been read.
cases.reason: The worker checks the message has reached the right person using the workplace's agreed steps.

worked_example_and_fade.situation: A worker is due at a made-up shop at 9:00. Their bus is late. They are safely waiting at the stop.
worked_example_and_fade.model: I must stay safe. I use the agreed way to tell the agreed contact: 'I am delayed. I may be late for 9:00. I will update you when I know more.' I follow the reply. This lets the team plan.
worked_example_and_fade.faded_example: A worker cannot come in today. 'I cannot come in today. I will follow ____.' This helps the team to ____.
worked_example_and_fade.answer: Follow the agreed absence steps. This helps the team plan or share the tasks.

adaptations.Cognition and Learning: Use two simple picture or word choices for late and away. Read clock times aloud so reading a clock is not the learning barrier. Keep the three-step prompt visible: stay safe, tell the agreed contact, follow the agreed steps.
adaptations.Communication and Interaction: Rehearse one message with an adult before a partner role play. Offer a written stem, pointing or a scribed response. Allow wait time and no public performance requirement.
adaptations.SEMH: Do not use real attendance, punctuality or health records. Use third-person workers. Avoid blame. Offer an observer role and a calm reset with a clear return task.
adaptations.Sensory and Physical: Use large print, uncluttered time cards and a seated role. Accept dictation or a scribe. Teach safe communication without requiring a real phone or travel task.
adaptations.EAL: Plan in any language. Contrast late and away with short examples. Accept a first-language rehearsal, then model one brief English message.

ta_focus.I do: Point to the safe contact steps and check the difference between delayed and absent.
ta_focus.We do: Prompt for a reason, not just a choice. Use made-up cases and avoid questions about the pupil's history.
ta_focus.Independent: Record whether the pupil can explain time, select a delay action and select an absence action. Note each prompt used and one next step.

prompt_ladder: 1 Point to the place or instruction. 2 Ask a short question. 3 Rephrase the instruction. 4 Provide a scaffold or choice. 5 Model the first step only, then return the task.

main_hinge.question: A worker will be late. What is the best action?
choices: B: Stay safe and tell the agreed contact as soon as possible.
main_hinge.reason: An early message helps the team plan. Being late does not make unsafe travel a good choice.
main_hinge.decision_rule: If any pupil chooses A or cannot explain B, model the contact message and safe travel step, then check with the parallel hinge.

parallel_hinge.question: A worker cannot come in today. What is the best action?
choices: A: Follow the agreed absence steps and tell the agreed contact.
B: Wait until the next day to say anything.
parallel_hinge.reason: The team needs timely information to change its plan.

success: I can say why being ready on time helps.
I can choose what to do if delayed.
I can choose what to do if absent.
evidence_prompts: Why being ready on time matters

evidence.description: Actual book/typed/pointed/oral response with date, work reference, access, supplied answers, first response, one NS and reply.

assessment: Record actual evidence against each outcome. Shown means evidence covers it with access logged. Partly means some parts shown. Not yet seen includes missing work or a pass; specify which. Do not count an adult model as independent work. Classroom practice is not proof of workplace competence.
private_help_route: Ask a trusted adult for a private talk. Point to HELP, write or use your aid. You may pass, pause and return with help. No personal story is needed.
typed_and_scribed_routes: Book, pointing, an aid, typing or an exact scribe are valid. Read back a scribed reply and allow a change. Record access apart from supplied answers. Plan in any language.

typed_route.heading: Type instead
typed_route.save: Use the usual save routine with lesson code and work reference; share privately.

feedback: VF verbal feedback; WS worked with support; I independent; NS next step; // self-edit; ? read back; E actual evidence saved; R responded. R follows Voice and Audience, one NS and the pupil reply in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. Add to Careers Portfolio. Offer to the Communication portfolio.
where_this_leads: Safe, clear messages about time help in future work, visits and work experience.
colour_blind_safe: Words and card IDs carry meaning. No colour-only codes.
accreditation: Evidence may contribute to the unit award. Staff confirm actual evidence and mapping; completion is not automatic.

Tuesday 2 March 2027 · P3 · 40 minutes · Year A
BUILD Careers · Spring 2 Week 2 · Public edition
Attendance, punctuality and reliability
Unit: Resilience & Change — Work-ready resilience
Theme: Resilience & Change. Five teaching weeks. Week 5 is the closing lesson and brings rows 26 and 27 together. Group: up to five learners. Supported is the default.
Exact lesson outcomes
I can explain why being on time matters and choose an appropriate action if I am delayed or absent.
Source: BUILD Careers scheme, Spring 2 rows 23. Focus and outcomes supplied verbatim in the current brief.
Prepare and purpose

Teach useful habits with invented, unnamed workplaces. Books, pens, Support Cards, Vocabulary Mat and Evidence Sheet. Print cards as reusable references. No write-on pupil sheets, internet, login or personal phone is needed. Read the exact outcome aloud and explain the short goal.
Where this leads: Safe, clear messages about time help in future work, visits and work experience.
Thread tags: SMSC S/So; British Values IL/MR. Respectful speech, a private choice of response and safe help-seeking are practised.
Forty minute sequence

table: In your book: write the title or ask for a scribe. Recall one work skill. Choose the time that gives the worker time to be ready.
Say: 'No. I stay safe and tell the agreed contact.'
Choose an action. Say: 'This helps because ...' Pick the best next step. Say one reason.
In your book: show why being on time helps. Show what to do if late. Show what to do if away.
Check my three answers. Add one detail if I need it. Finish: 'If I cannot be there on time, I will ... This helps ...'

blocks_in_document_order.paragraph: Teaching and checks
Arrival and retrieval 5 minutes

Use a calm check-in. Read the goal aloud. Explain that these are made-up work tasks, not pupils’ attendance records. Recall one work skill. Read aloud a 9:00 team start and arrivals of 8:55 and 9:10. Ask which gives time to get ready.
I Do 8 minutes

Model the delayed-worker example. Explain two effects of time: the team can plan and a task can start safely. Model telling the agreed contact as soon as safe, using the agreed way, and following the next instruction. Check: 'Must I rush or take a risk if I am late?'
We Do 10 minutes

Use the four scenario cards. For each, ask what the worker should do and why. Distinguish delay from absence. Rehearse a short factual message without personal or medical details. Ask the hinge question with simultaneous pointing or choice cards. If any pupil waits silently or chooses rushing, model a safe contact message and use the parallel hinge. If secure, remove the message stem for a new delay.
You Do 12 minutes
Offer the three routes. Require one reason why time matters, one delay action and one absence action. Let pupils dictate, draw or write in books. Record the support actually used.
Review and exit 5 minutes

Compare a silent delay with an early message. Ask which lets the team plan and why. Revisit the success criteria. Give each pupil one attainable next step. Ask the exit prompt. Record a short evidence note. Reinforce that illness and travel problems may happen; the taught skill is using safe, agreed communication, not blame.
Model and fade
I must stay safe. I use the agreed way to tell the agreed contact: 'I am delayed. I may be late for 9:00. I will update you when I know more.' I follow the reply. This lets the team plan.
A worker cannot come in today. 'I cannot come in today. I will follow ____.' This helps the team to ____.

I can explain why being on time matters and choose an appropriate action if I am delayed or absent.
Model and card answers
All workplace cases are invented. Accept equivalent safe language. Do not require a public performance or a personal history.
Card A
The team can plan and start the task together.
Other workers know who is there and can share the tasks safely.
Card B
When safe, tell the agreed contact as soon as possible, using the agreed way. Say they are delayed, give an arrival estimate only if known, and follow the reply.
A clear early message helps the team change its plan. The worker must not rush or guess a time.
Card C
Use the agreed absence steps and tell the agreed contact as soon as possible. Ask a trusted adult for support if needed.
The team needs to know the worker is absent. A pupil does not need to share private health details in this role play.
Card D
Follow the agreed next contact step when safe, or ask a trusted adult for help. Do not assume the message has been read.
The worker checks the message has reached the right person using the workplace's agreed steps.
Worked example and fade
I must stay safe. I use the agreed way to tell the agreed contact: 'I am delayed. I may be late for 9:00. I will update you when I know more.' I follow the reply. This lets the team plan.
Follow the agreed absence steps. This helps the team plan or share the tasks.
Judgement and safe delivery
Main hinge

A worker will be late. What is the best action? A: Say nothing and rush.  B: Stay safe and tell the agreed contact as soon as possible. Key B. An early message helps the team plan. Being late does not make unsafe travel a good choice.
Parallel hinge

A worker cannot come in today. What is the best action? A: Follow the agreed absence steps and tell the agreed contact.  B: Wait until the next day to say anything. Key A. The team needs timely information to change its plan.
If any pupil chooses A or cannot explain B, model the contact message and safe travel step, then check with the parallel hinge.
What to retain

Why being ready on time matters; Appropriate delay action or message; Appropriate absence action or message. Record the actual words or selections, first attempt, work reference, usual access, supplied choices and answers, one NS and reply. Spelling and handwriting are not the target.
Common errors
If I am late, I should run or take a risk. Stay safe. Tell the agreed contact as soon as safe and follow the agreed steps.
A late message and an absence message mean the same thing. A delay means I may arrive later. An absence means I cannot be there. Make the message clear.

blocks_in_document_order.paragraph: Teaching and checks
Arrival and retrieval 5 minutes

Use a calm check-in. Read the goal aloud. Explain that these are made-up work tasks, not pupils’ attendance records. Recall one work skill. Read aloud a 9:00 team start and arrivals of 8:55 and 9:10. Ask which gives time to get ready.
I Do 8 minutes

Model the delayed-worker example. Explain two effects of time: the team can plan and a task can start safely. Model telling the agreed contact as soon as safe, using the agreed way, and following the next instruction. Check: 'Must I rush or take a risk if I am late?'
We Do 10 minutes

Use the four scenario cards. For each, ask what the worker should do and why. Distinguish delay from absence. Rehearse a short factual message without personal or medical details. Ask the hinge question with simultaneous pointing or choice cards. If any pupil waits silently or chooses rushing, model a safe contact message and use the parallel hinge. If secure, remove the message stem for a new delay.
You Do 12 minutes
Offer the three routes. Require one reason why time matters, one delay action and one absence action. Let pupils dictate, draw or write in books. Record the support actually used.
Review and exit 5 minutes

Compare a silent delay with an early message. Ask which lets the team plan and why. Revisit the success criteria. Give each pupil one attainable next step. Ask the exit prompt. Record a short evidence note. Reinforce that illness and travel problems may happen; the taught skill is using safe, agreed communication, not blame.
